title: Why Australia's Million-Strong Indian Diaspora Is Reshaping Bilateral Ties With India
excerpt: A growing body of research and political attention positions Australia's Indian community — the country's fastest-growing large diaspora — as a strategic asset in one of the Indo-Pacific's most consequential partnerships.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Australia's Indian diaspora exceeds one million, becoming the largest source of skilled immigration.
  • The Albanese government invested A$16 million in the Maitri cultural program and a new economic roadmap.
  • 68% of Indian arrivals since 2006 hold a degree; their employment rate is 85.3%, above the migrant average.
  • The Indian diaspora is poised to be Australia's most politically influential since the Irish, according to experts.

  • Australia's Indian diaspora has surpassed one million people, making it the country's fastest-growing large migrant community and its largest source of skilled immigration.
  • The Albanese government has invested A$16 million to expand the Maitri cultural program and launched a new economic engagement roadmap identifying four growth areas: clean energy, education, agribusiness and tourism.
  • A landmark report from the University of Queensland and DFAT found 68 percent of Indian arrivals since 2006 hold an undergraduate degree or higher, with an employment rate of 85.3 percent — well above the migrant average.
  • Former UQ Chancellor Peter Varghese has said the Indian diaspora may become "the most politically influential diaspora in Australian history since the Irish."

Australia's Indian community has crossed the one-million mark, and both Canberra and New Delhi are treating this demographic shift as a strategic asset rather than just a migration statistic. A new analysis published by Organiser examines how the community has moved from the margins of Australia's multicultural story to the center of its foreign policy calculus.

The shift is visible at the highest levels. When Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Melbourne on July 9 for a "Melbourne Meets Modi" event, he was greeted by thousands of Indian Australians and his counterpart, Anthony Albanese, in a display that would have been unimaginable two decades ago.

"India-Australia relations have scaled new heights. The Indian diaspora has played a significant role in strengthening bilateral ties."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Melbourne, July 2026

The Numbers Tell the Story

A landmark report published by the University of Queensland in partnership with Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade offers the most comprehensive statistical portrait of the community to date. Its findings challenge stereotypes and underscore why policymakers on both sides are paying attention.

> **"Most first-generation migrants are between 25 and 44 years old — prime working age."**

"Its findings challenge stereotypes and underscore why policymakers on both sides are paying attention.</p> <p>Since 2006, the Indian-born population in Australia has grown 3.7-fold."

Since 2006, the Indian-born population in Australia has grown 3.7-fold. Most first-generation migrants are between 25 and 44 years old — prime working age. Sixty-eight percent arrive with an undergraduate degree or higher. Their employment rate stands at 85.3 percent, compared with 80 percent for migrants overall. Ninety percent live in capital cities, though regional areas are seeing rapid growth.

Indian students now represent the second-largest cohort of international research candidates in Australian universities, and education remains the primary pathway for new arrivals, with nearly half entering through study visas.

From Cultural Bridge to Strategic Asset

Former UQ Chancellor Peter Varghese, who also served as Secretary of DFAT and Australia's High Commissioner to India, has been among the most vocal advocates for rethinking the diaspora's role. In a series of public addresses, Varghese has argued that Australia needs to shift from viewing Indian Australians through a multicultural lens to treating them as a foreign policy and trade asset.

"The Indian diaspora may prove over the next two decades to be the most politically influential diaspora in Australian history since the Irish," Varghese has said, pointing to the community's growing presence in state politics and its potential to shape how Australian leaders prioritize the India relationship.

Investment in Cultural and Economic Ties
›A$16 million committed to Maitri cultural program.
›New economic roadmap identifies four growth areas.
›Focus areas: clean energy, education, agribusiness, tourism.
›18 bilateral outcomes from Modi's Melbourne visit.

The Albanese government appears to be listening. It has committed A$16 million to expand the Maitri program — Australia's flagship cultural and people-to-people initiative with India — and launched a new economic engagement roadmap built around four "superhighways of growth": clean energy, education and skills, agribusiness, and tourism.

The Economic Dimension

Modi's visit to Melbourne produced 18 bilateral outcomes spanning defense, maritime security and education. Senator Penny Wong, Australia's Foreign Minister, framed the economic push in strategic terms: "By boosting our economic ties with India, we are not only creating more jobs and opportunities for Australians, we are advancing our shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific."

Trade Minister Don Farrell was equally direct: "Australia has a rich and diverse Indian community, with strong personal and economic ties. The potential of our relationship with India is almost unmatched, opening a fast-growing market of over 1.4 billion people."

The roadmap identifies nearly 50 specific opportunities for deeper engagement, including defense industries, sports, space and technology — sectors where Indian Australians are already establishing professional networks that bridge the two economies.

What It Means for NRIs

For Indians considering migration or already settled in Australia, the political wind is favorable. The community's economic profile — highly educated, heavily employed, concentrated in growth sectors — gives it leverage that newer diaspora groups rarely possess. State-level political representation is growing, and the community's influence on federal policy toward India is becoming harder to ignore.

The challenge, as Varghese and others have noted, is converting numerical growth into institutional influence. Australia's Indian community is young, professionally successful and increasingly organized. Whether it can translate those advantages into the kind of durable political and cultural weight that other diaspora communities have built over generations will shape the Australia-India relationship for decades to come.
